They prefer the term “kill zone,” used to describe the 10- to 20-mile-wide no-man’s-land between the two armies. The reason for this conceptual shift is simple: Omnipresent drone surveillance has made it nearly impossible for anyone to get close to enemy-controlled territory without being detected.

According to recent reports, hollywood doesn’t seem to have gotten the memo. In a recent episode of the hit TV show Lioness, Zoe Saldaña’s character leads a small group of U.S. covert operators on a secret mission to capture an enemy spy who is hanging out with Russian forces in Ukraine. To do so, the Americans have to cross from the Ukrainian side to the Russian one—which they do by simply walking across, in broad daylight, tightly bunched together. In the real world, they would have been shredded by kamikaze drones or artillery as soon as they started their stroll. Plus, the sky above them is filled with so many drones that it calls to mind one of those spectacular drone light indicates. But that’s far from the modus operandi in Ukraine: You don’t need mega-swarms to keep a large area under surveillance; a bunch of individual operators searching in assigned sectors is enough. Compounding the absurdity, Saldaña’s character and her team only get attacked on their way back from their mission. Did it really take that long for the Russians to notice them?

But perhaps the makers of Lioness deserve some credit simply for tackling the subject. Four and a half years after the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion, cultural depictions of how the war is actually being fought are strikingly thin on the ground. A few journalists have written solid first-person accounts of the conflict, and documentary filmmakers, many of them Ukrainian, have explored it with astonishing intimacy. Yet their works have reached relatively small audiences. Where are the gripping stories for the broader public?

Combat drones have certainly made a mark on the broader culture. You see them everywhere, from movies like The Terminal List: Dark Wolf , where an assassin uses a drone to blow up a car, to the BBC’s police procedural Vigil, which includes a sequence in which military drones are turned against their own side by a hostile hacker. It’s striking how often drones turn up in dystopian science fiction films—such as The Gorge, where two snipers fight off autonomous drones, and The Outer Threat, in which a man with a dramatic secret has to protect his family from a hostile government equipped with drone swarms. A few years ago, the drone designs in these films probably would have resembled the exquisitely engineered aircraft of the so-called global war on terror. Now, even sci-fi creators seem to be favoring small quadcopters like the ones used by Ukrainians in their fight against Russia. But few of these cultural references involve depictions of war.

It has been revealed that retired Australian Army Maj. Gen. Mick Ryan, who has carefully tracked the war in Ukraine, argues that pop culture can be a useful way of helping politicians and the public stay abreast of developments on the battlefield. “Military doctrine is inaccessible to most people, including a lot of people in the military,” he said. “Whether it’s movies, television, books, or podcasts, [pop culture] can be an excellent way of making complex military and technological intersections accessible to a broader range of people.” Ryan practices what he preaches: He’s written an excellent speculative novel, White Sun War, about a hypothetical conflict over Taiwan, which includes detailed scenes of Chinese and U.S. forces fighting with the help of autonomous unmanned ground vehicles. Ryan’s fictional technology is ahead of what the Russians and Ukrainians have developed in their war—but only slightly.

Recent findings suggest that A Ukrainian soldier fires at a drone flying overhead in Kramatorsk, Ukraine, on Nov. 11. Kostiantyn Liberov/Libkos/Getty Images.

Could it be that drone warfare is just too complicated for compelling storytelling? By now, both sides in the Russia-Ukraine war have deployed a wide variety of drones on land, at sea, and in the air. None of these machines exists in isolation. They’re part of complex battlefield ecosystems that encompass reconnaissance, strike, and (increasingly) supply. Lately the Ukrainians have even been using ground drones to evacuate wounded soldiers. The intensity of the conflict has driven an astonishing pace of innovation, often involving the intricacies of maintaining reliable communications and targeting in environments saturated with electronic warfare measures. Responses have included drones controlled by fiber-optic cables (which can’t be jammed, unlike radio signals) and increasing reliance on artificial intelligence systems that can keep drones on target even when their links with operators go down.

In a recent development, perhaps it’s no surprise that outsiders have a hard time keeping up. In October, video game publisher Activision released Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, the latest installment of its long-running franchise. (A reminder: The global gaming industry is way bigger than the movie industry.) The story revolves around an imagined North Korean invasion of South Korea, and its depiction of the intense combat that such a conflict would entail is amazingly convincing. The game’s creators have put a huge amount of effort into getting the details right (even extending to hiring a dialect coach to consult on the different forms of Korean spoken by the characters).

Industry observers note that seeing the effort the game’s designers put into verisimilitude, it’s all the more surprising that drones have a very limited role. This omission is especially odd given that North Korea has dispatched large numbers of troops to help Russia in the war against Ukraine—in part so that Kim Jong Un’s forces could learn about the intricacies of drone warfare. The game’s creators seem to have been oblivious to this. When a joint South Korean-U.S. force counters the invasion with an amphibious counterattack, the intensity of the combat recalls the opening scenes of Saving Private Ryan. Yet neither side in the fight deploys drones on land or in the sky—although this is exactly the sort of combat in which modern militaries are already working frantically to incorporate the lessons of Ukraine.

In 1983, two movies sought to educate and alarm the public about the risks of upcoming technologies.

From the president on down, many Americans still do not grasp the implications of drones and other threats.

Sources indicate that part of the problem is surely that the remote-controlled, seemingly anonymous nature of modern drones diminishes their narrative potential. Real-life drone operations often involve long and meticulous searches and extended loitering—not exactly the stuff of high drama. Those brutal Ukrainian drone attack videos that now populate social media show only the climactic moments that follow hours and hours of painstaking preparation and reconnaissance. This could be why we see some video game designers creating drones with machine guns on them; in real life, that’s a generally useless approach, since the recoil from the guns would destabilize the drone, perhaps fatally. But shooting feels a lot more satisfying than hitting a distant target that you can only see on a screen.

That video games present such a distorted vision of contemporary war is especially ironic considering that the gaming industry has significantly shaped drone warfare. Military drone controllers are often modeled on the ones used by gamers, which hugely simplifies training.

Ukrainian filmmakers have found themselves confronting similar narrative challenges. The fascinating upcoming movie Killhouse, which was shot in close cooperation with the Ukrainian military, features plenty of scenes that convey a vivid sense of the peculiarities of drone warfare. The film turns on the fate of a civilian couple who are lured into the gray zone between the front lines by Russian gangsters who are holding their daughter for ransom. Unlike the blissful U.S. soldiers in Lioness, the desperate mother and father are immediately detected by both the Russians and Ukrainians as soon as they enter the area. The Russians promptly shell them, while the Ukrainians devise a complicated, drone-assisted strategy for their rescue—and, ultimately, the daughter’s. One particularly nail-biting sequence depicts an operator trying to use a drone to guide a character through a minefield, even though he has no clear way of communicating with her.

Sources indicate that the movie’s creators would have done well to stop there, after showing us real-life drones in real-life situations. Unfortunately, even they apparently felt the need to juice up their story by introducing a set of as-yet-non-existent drones that use facial recognition systems for their targets. (That capability is pretty useful for the Chinese surveillance state; why you would need it on a battlefield without expansive access to a database of enemy faces remains unclear.) At the moment of a critical showdown, these ultra-high-tech drones are used simply as brute force to knock out several Russian soldiers—all that fancy equipment ends up effectively serving the same purpose as a couple of substantial rocks.

Perhaps the shortcomings of movies and video games aren’t worth taking so seriously. There’s no requirement for ultra-realism, and no one should exaggerate the extent to which popular culture drives the decisions of policymakers. But is it just a coincidence that Western militaries, policymakers, and politicians are still failing to learn from the war in Ukraine after all these years?

A still from Killhouse. Ukrainian Film Division.

According to recent reports, U.S. and other Western military bases are still plagued by drone incursions of unknown provenance; the one thing that’s clear is that many of these drones, which are equipped to resist powerful jamming, aren’t operated by hobbyists. In recent weeks, the U.S. Air Force has cited the threat of drone attacks in connection with at least two major alerts at air bases in Britain. Decision-makers were apparently reacting to fears that Iran might launch an attack emulating Kyiv’s stunning Operation Spiderweb, when Ukraine managed to destroy a number of Russian strategic bombers by launching drones that were smuggled into Russia on freight trucks. European NATO members have experienced various drone incursions, as well as confronting actual attacks. Even the Australians have had to deal with mysterious drone sightings near their bases. The technology is proliferating; the problem can no longer be written off.

We’re still waiting for the Hollywood blockbuster that brings home the impact of drone warfare to ordinary voters—something like the 1927 film Wings, one of the first to familiarize a broad audience with the significance of military aircraft. But the lack of popular familiarity with the changed nature of war is no excuse for the complacency of Western leaders.

Christian Caryl is a columnist at Foreign Policy, a former Moscow bureau chief for Newsweek and U.S. News & World Report, and the author of Strange Rebels: 1979 and the Birth of the 21st Century. X: @ccaryl.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Intersolar & Energy Storage North America.

Industry observers note that in June 2026, Google and Voltus announced a three-year agreement to unlock up to 100 megawatts (MW) of distributed capacity annually in PJM. Under Voltus’s Bring Your Own Capacity model, Google funds procurement while Voltus aggregates qualifying distributed energy resources (DERs) and compensates participating customers.1.

In a recent development, the deal is one of three distinct paths to earn revenue from DERs. Across the U.S., utility programs, wholesale electricity markets, and bilateral contracts each have their own eligibility requirements, payment structures and commercial responsibilities.

Utility programs and procurement.

Recent findings suggest that utility programs offer an established pathway for compensating customers and asset owners who reduce demand, shift consumption or discharge stored energy during periods of grid need. Payments may be tied to enrollment, committed capacity, measured performance or a combination of these factors. Massachusetts, for example, offers residential battery customers $275 per kW of average summer performance through ConnectedSolutions2.

Beyond customer incentive programs, utilities also procure distributed flexibility through contracts to address local grid constraints or broader capacity needs. Unlike standardized incentives, these arrangements can establish specific delivery requirements and compensation terms, creating opportunities for developers and service providers to assemble and manage DER portfolios. During a July 2026 heat event, Green Mountain Power dispatched 90 MW of stored energy capacity, helping customers avoid an estimated $6 million in peak-related costs during one peak hour3.

Sources indicate that aggregated DERs can earn revenue from energy, capacity, and ancillary services in wholesale electricity markets, subject to regional market rules and resource qualification. Unlike utility-specific programs, wholesale markets can provide access to broader regional revenue opportunities and multiple grid services. For developers and installers, participation typically occurs through an aggregator or other qualified market participant rather than through direct market registration.

Recent findings suggest that while Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) Order 2222 established a broader framework for DER participation, uneven implementation across regional markets continues to constrain commercial opportunities for aggregated resources. Market access does not automatically translate into revenue, as individual resources must still meet qualification requirements and comply with market-specific rules. Upcoming York Independent System Operator (NYISO), for example, requires DER aggregations to meet minimum capacity and real-time telemetry requirements, which can increase participation costs and limit the economic viability of smaller resources.

It has been revealed that wholesale participation can also expose VPP portfolios to fluctuating market prices, performance obligations and restrictions on receiving compensation for overlapping services. In Texas, ERCOT’s Aggregate Distributed Energy Resource (ADER) pilot allows aggregated DERs to participate in wholesale energy and ancillary services markets, subject to qualification, telemetry, and dispatch requirements.

Bilateral contracts and emerging buyers.

Bilateral contracts allow utilities and large electricity consumers to procure distributed flexibility directly from aggregators and service providers. Growing interest from data center operators and other large energy buyers is expanding the potential market for VPP capacity beyond traditional utility programs. Unlike standardized programs, bilateral agreements can be tailored to a buyer’s specific needs, with negotiated terms for capacity, delivery periods, compensation, and performance obligations.

It has been revealed that the appropriate route depends on existing customer relationships, market access, and the responsibilities each partner assumes. Developers and EPCs working on commercial storage projects may find opportunities through utility procurement or capacity contracts, while residential installers with established battery customer bases may be well positioned to incorporate VPP enrollment into utility programs. Wholesale markets can expand revenue opportunities through aggregation partners, and bilateral contracts can create opportunities to develop resources around specific buyer needs.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

Why have recent U.S. presidents done such a poor job of thinking about the consequences of wars before they start them? And is it possible that rather than learning lessons from the past, our leaders are actually getting worse at this critical task—more impulsive, less thoughtful—while Congress and the public let them get away with it?

Industry observers note that these are questions that run like a baleful subplot through Secrets, the new memoir from Bob Woodward, the Washington Post investigative reporter who, by delivering stunning scoops through 11 presidencies over a half century, has become a Washington institution in his own right. In his new book, he reveals for the first time the many deep-background sources on which he based his reporting over the decades.

Industry observers note that why have recent U.S. presidents done such a poor job of thinking about the consequences of wars before they start them? And is it possible that rather than learning lessons from the past, our leaders are actually getting worse at this critical task—more impulsive, less thoughtful—while Congress and the public let them get away with it?

Secrets: A Reporter’s Memoir, Bob Woodward, Simon & Schuster, 592 pp., $35, November 2026.

In a recent development, these are questions that run like a baleful subplot through Secrets, the new memoir from Bob Woodward, the Washington Post investigative reporter who, by delivering stunning scoops through 11 presidencies over a half century, has become a Washington institution in his own right. In his new book, he reveals for the first time the many deep-background sources on which he based his reporting over the decades.

It has been revealed that woodward, of course, became famous as one half of the reporting duo that broke open the Watergate story (the other being Carl Bernstein), prompting the 1974 resignation of President Richard Nixon. Since then, he’s produced books on everything from the Supreme Court (The Brethren) to the doomed comedian John Belushi. But starting with his 1991 book, The Commanders, Woodward has spent a good part of his later career exploring what he calls “the most serious action a president can take”: declaring war.

It has been revealed that much has been written about President Donald Trump’s ill-justified war against Iran that began earlier this year, and whether his controversial defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, should bear the blame for giving Trump far-too-optimistic assurances of success. But this bumbling process, such as it was, has ample precedent going back to the Vietnam War. Time after time, presidents have botched it badly, Woodward writes, for almost always for the same reasons: a failure to thoroughly hash out the pitfalls before they pull the trigger, and a commensurate failure by their senior staff to deliver tough, honest assessments of the risks.

With a couple of exceptions, such as Brent Scowcroft, President George H.W. Bush’s national security advisor, or Colin Powell, George W. Bush’s first secretary of state, presidents rarely get the straight story from their advisors, Woodward writes.

According to recent reports, “I have seen clearly over a half century of reporting on 11 presidents how crucial it is that a president understand that part of their job is to find ways to puncture the treacherous curtain of deference around them,” he writes. “Others might call it Oval Office Freeze, not wanting to bring bad news to a president or framing something in a way that panders to their ego or worldview.”.

Sources indicate that this deep dysfunction, Woodward suggests, is the throughline from Lyndon Johnson in Vietnam, who was ill-served by his defense secretary, Robert McNamara, and other senior military officials; to George W. Bush, who was fraudulently persuaded to invade Iraq by Vice President Dick Cheney, Defense Secretary Donald Rumsfeld, and CIA Director George Tenet.

According to recent reports, U.S. President Lyndon B. Johnson and Defense Secretary Robert McNamara react during a meeting at the White House in Washington on Feb. 7, 1968. Yoichi Okamoto/Johnson White House Photographs/NARA/PhotoQuest/Getty Images.

In a recent development, trump’s ill-advised aggression against Iran—which has degenerated into a draining, nine-month conflict with no end in sight—is only the latest example of governmental ineptitude at the highest level, resulting in the unnecessary loss of innocent lives and a decline in U.S. prestige and power. Trump debuted “a destructive and bloody war with no legal authority,” Woodward writes. “His impulsive decision to start a war with Iran is the clearest example of what happens when there is no one to say, ‘Wait a minute, what are the consequences?’”.

What’s most unnerving, perhaps, is that this ego-driven impulse to launch unnecessary wars may have grown more haphazard at a time when war has grown more dangerous. AI-driven autonomous systems are increasingly coming to dominate command and control, and presidential decisions to respond to threats sometimes must be made in minutes or seconds. Under recent concepts like the Defense Department’s Joint All-Domain Command and Control—which connects all branches of the armed forces into a unified, AI-powered network—conventional and nuclear war strategy is being combined in new ways, experts say. And in an era when many missiles are “dual use,” strategists may not know if an incoming missile has a conventional or a nuclear warhead.

Beijing appears to be implementing similar systems, and despite the historic trilateral summit this week between Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, there are almost no negotiated restraints in place between the United States, China, and Russia.

Woodward writes that the threat of accidental nuclear war has haunted him since his earliest days. Just out of Yale on an ROTC scholarship in the mid-1960s, he served on a Navy communications ship designed as a relocation site for the president in the event of a national security emergency, especially nuclear war. Promptly he realized how easily the locks on the nuclear codes could be broken.

“I felt a little ill at the absurdity of it all—to have weapons of such destructive potential and to give me, a 22-year-old ensign, responsibility related to their use,” he writes. “My mind worried endlessly over the possible scenarios that could cause the nuclear procedures and safeguards to break down. What were the fatal flaws? There seemed to be far too many.”.

Later on, as a renowned reporter interviewing high-level U.S. officials, including McNamara and Secretary of State Henry Kissinger, Woodward says he came to realize how disturbingly real his early fears were. “Nuclear procedures were still a mess,” he writes. Woodward quotes McNamara—the erstwhile hawk who in retirement became an advocate for the abolition of nuclear weapons—as saying, “You could never control a nuclear war.”.

According to recent reports, today at age 83, Woodward indicates he’s still scared—perhaps more so. “At heart, I am still the shaken 22-year-old junior Navy officer who witnessed the weak locks on the safes guarding authentication codes for using US nuclear weapons and imagined how easily it could all go wrong,” Woodward writes. “I have always been a catastrophic thinker, but these days the dangers feel more present and grave.”.

Sources indicate that from right: U.S. President George W. Bush meets with Vice President Dick Cheney and Defense Secretary Donald Rumsfeld outside the White House Oval Office in Washington on March 19, 2003, shortly after authorizing Operation Iraqi Freedom. Eric Draper/White House/Getty Images.

Sources indicate that this theme of self-defeating war begins to emerge in Woodward’s book through an extraordinary series of interviews Woodward had with McNamara before the latter died in 2009. In excruciating detail, the anguished McNamara explains to Woodward why, during Vietnam, he failed utterly to insist on a “knock-down, drag-out debate over the loose assumptions, unasked questions and thin analyses underlying our military strategy.” McNamara astonishes Woodward by telling the reporter that not only was the U.S. military not “open in discussing their views with either the president or me,” McNamara himself didn’t really question the military at all.

“I don’t think the books today reviewing the Vietnam War give adequate attention to the failure of the senior military leaders to acquaint their civilian counterparts with their feelings that we were on a hopeless course” in Vietnam, McNamara said.

In a recent development, woodward’s response? “I was aghast,” he writes.

It has been revealed that but no fixes were ever put in place. On the contrary, as time went on, the decision-making process became even less systematic. Earlier this year, critics blasted Trump officials for saying he was attacking Iran because, as then-press secretary Karoline Leavitt said, “The president had a feeling … that Iran was going to strike the United States.” In fact, there was no evidence of a planned Iranian attack.

Warnings about transnational radicalism are rooted in the same accusations that sought to silence a renowned reporter decades ago.

The famous thinker’s newly introduced memoir reveals a fateful political and intellectual blind spot.

It’s the strategic disaster that keeps on giving.

Sources indicate that but how different was Trump’s “feeling” from Bush saying the decision to launch a preventive war against Iraq came from his “gut”? It isn’t, Woodward suggests.

Recent findings suggest that “In hindsight it is evident that not enough people got in Bush’s way. No one said, let’s slow down. What are we really trying to achieve here?” Woodward writes. As Bush told Woodward in an interview: “I’m not a textbook player, I’m a gut player.” Translation: The war in Iraq had no basis in careful analysis whatsoever.

Just as there is no record of Trump debating the wisdom of a new war against Iran with his national security team, McNamara concedes the same was largely true of Vietnam.

“The [Joint Chiefs of Staff] never really discussed the military proposal for Vietnam,” he told Woodward. “I don’t think you’ll find any record, secret or otherwise, of the chiefs’ critical analysis of the military plans in Vietnam.” As McNamara later admits, the Vietnam War had nothing to do with the superpower conflict between the United States and Soviet Union or the “domino theory” of the Cold War but was, instead “a civil war, not an external war.” It was, as Woodward writes, “In effect a no-win policy.”.

Sources indicate that mcNamara points to a map of Vietnam during a news conference in Washington on April 26, 1965. Marion S Trikosko/PhotoQuest/Getty Images.

Similarly, when it came to examining the premises of the Iraq invasion, “McNamara’s lesson was once again ignored.” There is no record that the Bush team ever held a serious debate about the wisdom of going into Iraq.

Recent findings suggest that “I could not help but think of Vietnam,” Woodward writes about the Iraq invasion. Bush, pressed repeatedly by Woodward, reveals in a series of interviews not long after the war began in 2003 that he had no real justification for his world-altering decision to attack Iraq other than the idea that Saddam, “given his nature,” might have pursued weapons of mass destruction.

Sources indicate that “I look back on this now more than 20 years later and realize his answer was preposterous,” Woodward writes. “I should have pressed him more on this. A leader’s ‘nature’ was not sufficient grounds for invading a country.”.

It has been revealed that nor was there even any longer much “anguish” over the possibility of making a wrong decision, as there was during Vietnam. Woodward writes that he told McNamara in one of their interviews that he tried to find evidence of “anguished memos” about Iraq similar to the ones McNamara had secretly written about Vietnam in 1967.

Industry observers note that the Bush team’s response? “‘There’s no anguish,’ they said. ‘Well, that’s what’s wrong with them,’ McNamara declared. ‘I’ll tell you, because there ought to be anguish.’” Woodward writes: “I did not respond but I agreed fully—more anguish might have stopped the war.”.

U.S. President Donald Trump, flanked by CIA Director John Ratcliffe (left), Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth (right), and Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Dan Caine (far right), addresses a news conference at the White House on April 6.Andrew Harnik/Getty Images.

According to recent reports, in his typical fashion, as he’s done through most of the 24 books he’s produced, Woodward plays the pure reporter who does little historical analysis and rarely passes judgment. Though in his last book, War, he called Trump  “the most reckless and impulsive president in history,” he doesn’t repeat that assessment here. Indeed, Woodward relates most of these conversations without giving any real historical context at all.

Nor does Woodward allow himself much, if any, psychological analysis of the historic figures he’s spent so many hours with. For example, he reports on his conversations with Joe Biden, in which the then-vice president notes the military was overselling President Barack Obama on the war in Afghanistan and boasts, “The military doesn’t fuck around with me.”.

But it seems clear that it was Biden’s overconfidence in his own judgment that led him, as president, to ignore accurate assessments from his own military advisors about the rapid collapse of the Afghan government and subsequent takeover by the Taliban in 2021.

Still, Woodward does tend toward some broad conclusions. He quotes the late historian David McCullough as saying that the greatest acts of presidents involve not going to war.

Sources indicate that “The examples he gave me all shared one element: restraint. The most vital decision John Adams made was not to go to war with France, McCullough told me.” Similarly, Dwight Eisenhower’s “greatest series of decisions was keeping United States troops out of Vietnam.”.

Recent findings suggest that U.S. President John F. Kennedy meets with military leaders in the Oval Office on Oct. 16, 1962, to discuss surveillance of Cuba. Charles Phelps Cushing/ClassicStock/Getty Images.

Again quoting McNamara, Woodward also notes that John F. Kennedy, unusually for a president, defied the majority of his national security team when they voted in favor of attacking Cuba during the 1962 Cuban missile crisis—voting, in effect, to go to war with the USSR. “The vote is 9 to 8 in favor of attacking and destroying the missiles, Kennedy confirmed to the group, and without pausing stated as clear as a bell, ‘The eights have it,’” Woodward quotes McNamara as saying.

He concludes: “Looking back, the world was safer because President Kennedy believed his primary responsibility as commander in chief of the most powerful military in the world was to avoid war where possible.”.

Michael Hirsh is a columnist for Foreign Policy. He is the author of two books: Capital Offense: How Washington’s Wise Men Turned America’s Future Over to Wall Street and At War With Ourselves: Why America Is Squandering Its Chance to Build a Better World. X: @michaelphirsh.

#76719. The Only Way to End the Netanyahu Era

The Only Way to End the Netanyahu Era

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2532 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • AYMAN ODEH served in the Knesset from 2015 to 2026.
  • Arab Citizens of Israel Can Bring Change, but They Can’t Do It Alone.
  • As the Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot struggles to assemble a governing coalition following last month’s elections, Israel finds itself in a familiar political predicament.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AYMAN ODEH served in the Knesset from 2015 to 2026. He is the former leader of the Joint List and the Hadash party.

Arab Citizens of Israel Can Bring Change, but They Can’t Do It Alone.

As the Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot struggles to assemble a governing coalition following last month’s elections, Israel finds itself in a familiar political predicament. The parties opposed to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his far-right coalition command a clear majority in the Knesset, with 67 of its 120 seats. Yet the four Jewish-led parties in Eisenkot’s camp hold just 48 seats, leaving them unable to form a government on their own. The impasse echoes the prolonged political deadlock between 2019 and 2021, when Netanyahu’s supporters and his opponents remained locked in competing parliamentary blocs, and four consecutive elections failed to produce a stable governing majority.

Industry observers note that but one thing is different this time. Israel’s Arab-led parties, the Joint List and Raam, are stronger than ever. Powered by extraordinary turnout among Arab citizens of Israel, they won a record 19 seats in the Knesset: 11 for the Joint List and eight for Raam. This political mobilization is vital in itself, demonstrating Arab voters’ overwhelming desire for change and their recognition of the importance of participating in elections. But its significance goes far beyond the number of seats they have won. Together, the Arab parties now have the potential to be a decisive force in an anti-Netanyahu coalition, providing the parliamentary backing needed to form a government. The proof of this power has already been shown: on November 17, Arab support was crucial in the vote to replace the Likud speaker of the Knesset with a speaker from Eisenkot’s party. Now they have a historic opportunity to put the country on a different path.

According to recent reports, as the first and former leader of the Joint List, I know how much is at stake. In 2019, I helped lead a groundbreaking effort to give Arab-led parties a direct voice in the Israeli political system. We took an enormous political risk by endorsing Benny Gantz, then a former chief of staff of the Israeli military and Netanyahu’s principal rival, as a candidate to form a government. We did so despite our profound political and ideological differences with him. Although that effort ultimately fell short, with Gantz choosing to pursue a “unity government” with Netanyahu instead, it established an vital precedent: by showing a willingness to work with Jewish political forces with whom they had deep disagreements, parties representing the Arab public had a real chance to prevent a Netanyahu-led far-right government from holding power.

Today, after nearly four years of disastrous leadership by Netanyahu and his far-right allies, that possibility has become far more urgent. It will take political courage on both sides. Eisenkot must be able to offer something to the Arab-led parties, and the Arab-led parties will need to be comfortable offering support to a government that they may not agree with on many complications. But the remarkable Arab turnout and the sizable Israeli majority that is now against Netanyahu have pointed to a way forward. Not only Israel’s future but also its place in the region and the world may depend on the willingness of its leaders to engage with the country’s Palestinian minority. Ultimately, such a partnership will be essential to building the trust between Jews and Arabs that is a prerequisite to achieving any real progress toward a viable Israeli-Palestinian peace. This is the real choice now facing Israel: whether Israelis are prepared to replace the politics of supremacy and exclusion with a politics of equality.

It has been revealed that the factors that drove record numbers of Palestinian citizens of Israel to the polls in October have been years in the making. Although the country’s Arab citizens make up more than 20 percent of the Israeli electorate and have long made vital contributions to Israeli society as doctors, lawyers, engineers, high-tech professionals, and in many other fields, the Israeli right has for decades demonized them as enemies: a fifth column and a threat to the state. In recent years, this hostility has increasingly manifested itself in harassment and open racism at universities and workplaces, in the media, in the parliament, and in everyday life.

Yet it would be a mistake to assume that Arab exclusion has been driven only by Netanyahu and the radical right. Zionist parties of the center and the left have also contributed, by keeping a distance from Arab voters or simply ignoring them. The belief that Jewish citizens should ultimately determine the country’s political direction while Arab citizens must remain within whatever limits have been set for them runs deep in Israeli politics. Netanyahu understood early on how to turn this contradiction into a political strategy. Since the 1990s, he has repeatedly used the same formula: inciting his supporters against Arab citizens, delegitimizing Arab representatives in parliament, and convincing Jewish Israelis that a government that relies on Arab political support would somehow be illegitimate.

These tactics proved to be among Netanyahu’s most effective political tools, especially given that Arab-led parties have long been some of his biggest foes. He didn’t need to convince everyone to support his Likud party or its various coalition partners. He only needed to convince enough people, including Jewish Israelis who opposed him, that working with Arab-led parties was dangerous and unacceptable. Netanyahu’s strategy also helped suppress Arab turnout. Since the Arab-led parties had little chance of changing the status quo, Arab voters had little incentive to vote: for many years, a significantly lower proportion of Arab citizens went to the polls than did their Jewish counterparts.

Recent findings suggest that that began to change in 2015 with the creation of the Joint List, which for the first time brought together four parties representing the Arab public on a single electoral ticket and which became the third-largest faction in the Knesset. By embracing a broader vision for our society, grounded in Jewish-Arab solidarity and opposition to the racism of the right, the Joint List demonstrated that Palestinian citizens of Israel could play a new and more influential role in the country’s political system. Then, under my leadership in 2019, the Joint List decided to back Gantz’s bid to unseat Netanyahu. The decision was highly controversial, both within the Arab electorate and across Israeli society. Many Arab voters were deeply ambivalent about supporting a potential government led by a former army chief whose political positions, particularly on the status of Palestinian citizens of Israel and the occupation, differed sharply from their own. Nevertheless, we were prepared to take that political risk because we understood that defeating Netanyahu was more crucial.

According to recent reports, in practice, our willingness to cooperate with the Zionist opposition was not, in fact, reciprocated. The Jewish opposition parties wanted our votes but could not bring themselves to accept us as equal political partners. And, ultimately, Gantz decided to form a government with Netanyahu instead. Nevertheless, the experience revealed that Jewish-Arab political cooperation could open up new horizons for a large segment of the public. Since then, every time that Arab-led parties have recommended or supported the effort of a Jewish candidate to form a government, or whenever the Israeli center-left has depended on their support, additional segments of Israeli society have become more open to this kind of cooperation.

In 2021–22, an Arab party, Raam, joined the short-lived government led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid. I had serious reservations about the model of partnership that emerged, which seemed to rest on the expectation that Arab political representatives would limit their involvement to civilian and domestic matters, while refraining from addressing political and national questions, particularly the occupation and the Palestinian issue. I reject this distinction. We are part of the Palestinian people, and our identity and political concerns cannot be separated from our citizenship in Israel.

Industry observers note that but these kinds of slow and painful steps are how political change often happens in national struggles. It does not always begin with a moral or democratic awakening. Sometimes, it begins with pragmatic necessity. When there is no other option, people begin to reconsider what had once been seen as impossible. In the current election, that dynamic has become even more important. After the unending crisis of the past four years, many Israeli voters, including both Arabs and Jews as well as the leaders of most of the Zionist opposition parties, have concluded that getting rid of the Netanyahu government is more necessary than ever.

It has been revealed that in recent past elections, voter turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel has generally remained between 50 and 60 percent. What explains the unprecedented 20-percentage-point surge in turnout in the October election? Three developments stand out: the war of annihilation in Gaza and the killing of tens of thousands of Palestinians; the daily racism and hostility that Arab citizens now face in the streets, in public spaces, and in virtually every aspect of their lives; and the crime that has spiraled out of control in Arab communities under the national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, whose policies have allowed it to flourish, and the relentless settler violence against Palestinians in the West Bank enabled by Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich. All the grief and frustration accumulated over these years were brought to the ballot box.

But there was another crucial factor as well. In the run-up to the election, Arab citizens, following the nearly even polls between Eisenkot and Netanyahu, could see in black and white just how much the outcome would depend on them. Voting this time would be more than a political choice. It was for many a personal responsibility and a way of taking control of their own future. That is why hundreds of thousands of Palestinian citizens of Israel made their way to the polls, defying years of efforts to silence them and undermine their political agency. Many understood that the future direction of the country might be quite literally in their hands.

Sources indicate that I saw elderly people, like my friend Jumah from Jisr al-Zarqa, taking to the streets and campaigning for the Joint List. Many of them had lived through the 1948 nakba, or “catastrophe,” which accompanied Israel’s establishment and involved terrible massacres, the destruction of hundreds of Palestinian villages and towns, and the displacement of around 750,000 Palestinians. I saw young people debating politics in the cafes and restaurants of my beloved Haifa, persuading their friends to vote. I saw women and men from Nazareth, Umm al-Fahm, Sakhnin, Rahat, Akko, Kafr Yasif, Majd al-Krum, and countless other towns and villages united by a shared sense of purpose. I saw political consciousness become a living, collective force. For a moment, the boundaries between generations and communities seemed to disappear.

According to recent reports, the result marks a remarkable advance of the process of Arab participation in the Israeli political system that began in 2019. In this election, Arab citizens of Israel turned out in record numbers, dramatically narrowing the historical turnout gap with Jewish voters. And that has made another political reality increasingly clear: Israel’s liberal and centrist camp cannot form a government without the parties that represent the Arab public. If it excludes them, as well as the ultra-Orthodox and the far right, it will not reach the 61 seats needed. This is the demographic reality. Israeli Jews who oppose Netanyahu must decide whom they are willing to build a political future with.

In a recent development, the debate about what Eisenkot should do and whether he should ask for Arab support is now unfolding beyond the Knesset, in people’s homes, cafés, in universities, and on the street. It is a deeply controversial question, and many Israelis disagree strenuously about it. Yet for the Arab-led parties, gaining sufficient importance to be able to provoke these conversations is an achievement. The fact that this debate is even taking place shows how the political process has caused Israelis to consider possibilities that until recently seemed unimaginable.

According to recent reports, in the end, Eisenkot may have few other options if he wants to replace Netanyahu, as he has promised. In most cases, political parties support coalitions to advance positive changes and achieve concrete goals. But there are moments when political cooperation is necessary for a different reason: to prevent something far worse. The most immediate and overriding objective today is to bring an end to the far-right Netanyahu government. That is a priority on which both the Zionist opposition and the Arab-led parties can agree.

Beyond this shared basic goal, the Arab-led parties should use their political influence to work on two levels. First, they must seek tangible improvements in their constituents’ lives: combating organized crime in Arab communities, securing budgets, addressing the housing crisis, ending the brutal treatment of Palestinians living under occupation in the West Bank, and pushing for a permanent cease-fire and the reconstruction of Gaza. These are fundamental issues of human dignity and civilian life. On a broader level, they should continue to push for real progress on Israeli-Palestinian peace that is ultimately based on two states coexisting, side by side.

Sources indicate that I do not expect the current Israeli political establishment to embrace these positions, but that does not mean that the Arab parties should not raise them at every opportunity. At the same time, the Arab parties can use their newfound political clout to build alliances between Jews and Arabs around shared political and strategic goals. The resulting partnerships must be about more than parliamentary arrangements; it must also create the foundations for a different future. That will require Jewish and Arab citizens of Israel to engage with one another on the basis of equality, rather than mere political convenience.

Thus far, Eisenkot has given few indications that he is prepared to go down this path. Since the election, it has been encouraging to see him condemn Netanyahu for fueling what he described as a “racist and violent” campaign against Israel’s Arab citizens. Yet many of the mainstream Zionist parties in Eisenkot’s camp have vowed not to work with the Arab parties. Still, Eisenkot must consider what that would mean. Thirty years from now, people will ask how Jewish supremacy became so normalized that even politicians who called themselves democrats accepted the exclusion of one-fifth of their fellow citizens. They will ask why Israel’s opposition could recognize the danger posed by Netanyahu’s government but not confront the assumptions that made his politics possible.

Industry observers note that there is an irony in the fact that, in a country that seeks to keep political hegemony exclusively in Jewish hands, the Palestinian minority, after decades of struggle for political recognition and equal rights, has emerged as one of the most significant forces shaping the country’s political future. We have come to understand that we must be courageous and cooperate with the Zionist parties of the center and left in order to oust Netanyahu, Ben-Gvir, and Smotrich. The question now is: Do these parties, which call themselves democratic and liberal, have the same courage?

Industry observers note that the biggest single media event of the decade took place on Thursday, and most of Washington missed it. Grand Theft Auto VI, the latest installment of the most popular video game series in the world, racked up nearly $1.5 billion in sales even before it rolled out, already making back what may have been a more-than-a-billion dollar budget. In the next week, total sales are projected to hit over $3 billion. The previous game in the series still makes half a billion dollars a year through its online version alone. (For comparison purposes, Taylor Swift’s Eras tour, the biggest concert tour of all time, took in just over $2 billion, while Avengers: Endgame grossed roughly $2.9 billion.).

In a recent development, video games are cultural juggernauts, and governments have noticed. As industry consultant George Osborn points out in his fresh book, Power Play: Video Games, Politics, and the Battle for Global Influence, video gaming, once a solitary activity, has become a largely communal one. Online play creates a “third place” where people, especially the young, can mingle. As Osborn puts it, “what happens in video games communities bleeds out into reality—all the way into our political discourse.”.

Recent findings suggest that power Play: Video Games, Politics, and the Battle for Global Influence, George E. Osborn, Prometheus, 376 pp., July 2026, $34.95.

Video games are cultural juggernauts, and governments have noticed. As industry consultant George Osborn points out in his newly introduced book, Power Play: Video Games, Politics, and the Battle for Global Influence, video gaming, once a solitary activity, has become a largely communal one. Online play creates a “third place” where people, especially the young, can mingle. As Osborn puts it, “what happens in video games communities bleeds out into reality—all the way into our political discourse.”.

According to recent reports, under Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, for instance, Saudi Arabia has become a major force in video games, mostly through the power of capital. The prince, himself a keen gamer, is trying to encourage the creation of a domestic industry. He’s had little success so far, but Saudi money has succeeded in buying up existing companies, such as the giant Electronic Arts for $55 billion and the manufacturer that created Pokémon Go for $3.5 billion.

According to recent reports, mohammed bin Salman wants to make money. But, as Osborn points out, he also wants to get gullible or greedy Westerners to help whitewash his corrupt, misogynistic autocracy. Buying gaming companies may be a more expensive route than donating to D.C. think tanks, but also perhaps a more effective one. Some industry insiders have already flagged worries about Saudi censorship in their games.

An artist rendering of “The Line” in an undated image. NEOM.

But if the Saudi government is shaping video games, the influence is going the other way as well. Consider some of the crown prince’s grandiose projects. His plan for The Line, a 106-mile-long and 650-foot-wide city, appeared to be inspired by the futuristic cities that appear in games like Cyberpunk 2077 and Deus Ex. The difference, of course, was that in reality The Line project was suspended after only 1.5 miles of foundation were dug.

That feedback loop between gaming and reality is also evident when looking at another of Osborn’s case studies, Russia. Especially since the invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Russian studios have churned out propaganda games such as Squad 22: ZOV, which Osborn describes as an “objectively bad video game” but also a hub for anti-Ukrainian memes and a gathering place for ultranationalists.

It has been revealed that the fantasies of Russian games hook back into wider influence efforts. With the help of influencers such as streamer GrishaPutin, these games aim to boost morale and recruitment while also luring in foreign fighters, roughly 11,000 of whom have died fighting on the Russian side. Australian Daryl Fladung has been missing, believed dead, for several months after being recruited to come and fight for Russia (and post propaganda videos) through online war games. His last videos show him terrified and in pain.

Australian Daryl Fladung (right) and two fellow Russia-supporting British nationals on arrival in Moscow in an undated photo. Telegram: Ben Stimson.

In a recent development, russia’s reactionary politics are also attractive to some gamers. The gender split in gaming is roughly equal nowadays but the third place of popular games has a habit of becoming dominated by the loudest young men. It’s not uncommon for female players to conceal their gender, or even use a voice changer, to avoid harassment.

That too has bled back into politics. Video game writers are generally liberal progressives, and there was a big push toward broadening representation in games in the 2010s, with female protagonists and people of color becoming more normalized. This was welcomed by many gamers but prompted a reactionary fury from others. The movement that resulted was Gamergate, which became part of the far-right’s attempt to woo younger male voters, with the encouragement of Steve Bannon. While it may have helped tip elections toward Donald Trump, it failed to produce any good games of its own.

It has been revealed that despite being the biggest video game market in the world, compared to Moscow, Beijing is far more reluctant to throw its weight around in gaming propaganda overseas. That’s in part because of a puritan communist dislike of any form of fun, leading to repeated crackdowns on minors playing games online and long delays before new games are officially approved.

Censorship at home is massive but, as Osborn notes, “Chinese games businesses invested billions of dollars in games businesses across the world to soften the blows landing on them from the CCP.” (pg. 151). Apart from some policing around Hong Kong and Taiwanese representation in games, those investments have mostly remained business-focused rather than trying to impose political limits. As with much else, China’s focus has been domestic control first, and foreign influence second.

The Honor of Kings International Championship in Shenzhen, China, on Dec. 3, 2022. Honor of Kings, a multiplayer online battle arena game, is operated by Tencent, China’s largest video game publisher.Honor of Kings/Tencent.

But perhaps gaming’s biggest global influence lies in its role driving the AI industry, a story Osborn doesn’t cover in depth because much of it is so recent. Gaming depends on video cards, which are built with the high-end chips that also fuel the AI revolution. In fiscal year 2018, for instance, Nvidia made roughly 57 percent of its income from gaming. Last year, that figure was 7 percent, with roughly 90 percent coming from AI data centers.

Sources indicate that osborn highlights the role gaming played in driving forward the innovation needed for newer and better technology, especially in chip design. But the shift of the industry toward AI has left gamers deeply angry at Nvidia, a organization they once adored. (As a result, some of the best investigative reporting on Jensen Huang’s fall and Nvidia’s role in evading U.S. sanctions on China has come out of the games media.) Gaming hardware used to be getting cheaper and cheaper; the same setup would be half the price two years later. Thanks to the AI race, the reverse is now true. The gaming PC I bought for $1,600 the week Trump was elected for a second time, anticipating tariff rises, now retails at $2,600. It might seem a little silly to care deeply about your toys getting more expensive. But the contestation between gamers and AI companies is a microcosm of a wider issue: Who controls technological power?

According to recent reports, screen captures of the survival horror game Resident Evil Requiem, released in February, showing Nvidia’s new graphics rendering model DLSS 5. It uses AI to infuse pixels with photorealistic lighting and materials. NVIDIA.

Recent findings suggest that personal computers have been the domain of tinkerers and inventors since they were first introduced at home. Now Sam Altman has put forward, then rapidly retracted, the idea that having RAM sitting in your own PC is “terrible” because it should be used by mega-corporations instead. In this context, the growing revolt against AI in video games—with players boycotting games that use AI art, AI writing, or even AI code—feels like part of something bigger.

Osborn’s final chapters are dedicated to promoting games that educate citizens and support the fight for democracy worldwide, from pro-Ukrainian stories to “green game jams” to promote climate awareness. But as long as the industry, and the technology that powers it, is in the hands of autocrats and tech tycoons, these aren’t the games we’ll be playing.

James Palmer is a deputy editor at Foreign Policy. Bluesky: @beijingpalmer.bsky.social.

He claims the outcome of the 2026 elections — where Democrats' sweeping victories in traditional red strongholds helped them reclaim majorities in the House and Senate — was a sign of voters rejecting Trump more than rebuking his policies.

"I think the thing we're missing is that it was really targeted at President Trump. I don't think it was targeted at the policies so much," Brownback told Fox News Digital in an interview. "Pride comes before a fall and a haughty spirit before a stumble.".

REPUBLICANS TURN ON TRUMP AFTER DEVASTATING MIDTERM LOSSES HAND DEMOCRATS CONTROL OF CONGRESS.

He suggested voters' frustrations extended beyond the economy to Trump's approach to governing.
